standard: RFC 8259 — The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

entries.title: RFC 8259 allows any JSON value at the top level
entries.body: Unlike RFC 4627, RFC 8259 permits any JSON value (object, array, number, string, true, false, null) as the top-level document. Parsers that only accept objects/arrays are non-compliant with RFC 8259.

entries.title: Object member names SHOULD be unique
entries.body: RFC 8259 says names within an object SHOULD be unique. Duplicate keys are technically valid JSON but behavior is implementation-defined (most parsers keep the last; some error). Never emit duplicate keys in production payloads.

entries.title: JSON has no integer/float distinction; no NaN or Infinity
entries.body: RFC 8259 numbers are decimal digit sequences with no required fraction/exponent; there is no separate integer type. NaN and Infinity are NOT valid JSON numbers. JavaScript Number precision is limited to 2^53-1 safe integers.

entries.title: The JSON grammar has no comments
entries.body: RFC 8259 defines no comment production. // and /* */ are parse errors in strict JSON. Adding comments requires a non-standard preprocessing step before parsing.

entries.title: Insignificant whitespace is space, tab, LF, CR
entries.body: Whitespace allowed between tokens: space (0x20), horizontal tab (0x09), line feed (0x0A), carriage return (0x0D). A literal newline inside a string must be escaped as \n, not left raw.

entries.title: Strings use \uXXXX escapes for control and surrogate pairs
entries.body: RFC 8259 strings are Unicode code points; control characters must be escaped. A literal newline inside a string is invalid—use \n. Surrogate pairs encode astral characters; lone surrogates are ill-formed.

entries.title: Only false, null, true literals (lowercase)
entries.body: RFC 8259 defines exactly three literals: false, null, true, all lowercase. TRUE, False, NULL, None, and undefined are NOT valid JSON and must be rejected by conforming parsers.

entries.title: Leading zeros are not allowed in numbers
entries.body: RFC 8259 forbids leading zeros in numbers (e.g. 01). The integer part must start with a non-zero digit (1-9) or be a single 0. Values like 1.0 and 0.5 are valid; 01 is not.

entries.title: RFC 8259 obsoletes RFC 7159 and RFC 4627
entries.body: RFC 8259 (Dec 2017) obsoletes RFC 7159 and RFC 4627. ECMA-404 defines the same grammar via a different formalism; discrepancies between them are tracked jointly by IETF and ECMA.

entries.title: Array element types need not be uniform
entries.body: RFC 8259 imposes no requirement that array elements share a type. Heterogeneous arrays are valid JSON; schema validation (not the grammar) enforces homogeneity when needed.
